newsitem.title: CANADA: Victims and bureaucrats look at land mine ban.
newsitem.headline: Victims and bureaucrats look at land mine ban.

text.p: The land mine was only the size of a small matchbox, a curious-looking object lying on the ground near Mohammad Usman Fitrat's house in Afghanistan.
When the 11-year-old boy picked it up, it blew off his hands and forearms and blasted out his left eye.

Now, 11 years later at an international conference in Ottawa on pushing for a global ban on land mines, he listens bemusedly and with a touch of bitterness when countries like Russia suggest they may still want to use the deadly weapons.

"Why would they need it? Because they have another war ahead? Another invasion?" said Mohammad, who had watched columns of Soviet tanks rumble by his village 20 miles (30 km) from the capital Kabul after its 1979 invasion.

"If they're aiming to invade, they shouldn't be killing civilians to depopulate," he said. "They should hit the military. Innocent civilians have nothing to do with the war. Innocent children have nothing to do with the war."
Mohammad now has two stumps for arms, just several inches (centimetres) below the elbow. Doctors split one forearm so that it can grasp, much like a lobster's claw. His left eye is plastic.
He has managed to go through school and college, specializing in computers even if it is difficult to strike keys precisely, and volunteers now for the Afghan Campaign to Ban Land Mines.
Afghans are expert on the subject. Some 400,000 of them have been maimed -- about one in 40 -- on top of countless others killed by mines.
Mohammad brought a human face and some urgency to the discussions by bureaucrats at the Oct. 3-5 conference.
About 25,000 people, mostly civilians, are killed or maimed by some of the 110 million mines around the world.

Organizers want to get negotiations started on a ban on anti-personnel land mines as quickly as possible and were encouraged by the commitment to that end by the 49 full participants -- more than double original expectations -- as well as the attendance of 24 observers.
But they also know the sluggish pace of multilateral arms negotiations, and that nations like the United States will be insisting on a large number joining, including the major ones.
Countries like Israel and South Korea maintain mines are still useful for defending their borders, but at this conference Iran signaled its readiness to forego the mines.
China, which experts say exports $3 land-mine specials to many parts of the developing world, was not part of it and Washington would clearly insist that it and Russia join.
Russian representative Viatcheslav Sergueev told Reuters his country did not support an immediate ban but saw significance in its attendance as an observer.
"The idea of a total ban is a rather new one, and we are here to see how those countries which support it are moving forward," he said.

A U.S. ambassador to the conference, Karl Inderfurth, said China had at least joined the U.N. General Assembly consensus in the past two years in adopting a resolution calling for the "eventual elimination" of land mines.

He said he hoped the Chinese would now be persuaded to allow consensus on the next step at the General Assembly, a resolution Washington would introduce at the end of the month to start negotiations "as quickly as possible."

The conference in Ottawa was likely to issue a similar call as a prelude to the U.N. discussions. Some have called for a treaty by 2000 but U.S. Ambassador Thomas McNamara said they would push merely for swift negotiations.
